source.title: Dense SAE Latents Are Features, Not Bugs
source.authors: Xiaoqing Sun; Alessandro Stolfo; Joshua Engels; Ben Wu; Senthooran Rajamanoharan; Mrinmaya Sachan; Max Tegmark

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. There is a stray MathJax loading message and some figure content is flattened, but the main text and relevant table values are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies SAE feature geometry in language models and refines the claim that SAE latents are canonical, stable units: it reports context-dependent latents and cautions that learned bases may not align with the true feature basis. It also directly measures antipodal pairing and its dependence on SAE architecture.
record.gate_note: The paper tests real-model SAE feature structure, including whether dense latents reflect model representations, whether dense latents pair to represent one-dimensional directions, and whether SAE latents behave as stable semantic units. The context-binding steering is an induced intervention, so it is evidence about latent function under steering, not about the frequency of that behavior without intervention. The paper's citations and introductory discussion of toy-model superposition are not results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study tests, in Gemma 2 2B, GPT-2 and LLaMA-3.2-1B SAEs, whether dense SAE latents track real residual-stream structure (V4). It also tests whether some latents lack a stable, globally consistent meaning, and whether their geometry depends on SAE architecture (V5). It argues that some model features are intrinsically dense, which qualifies the sparse-feature framing. It runs no toy models and no neuron-capacity tests.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that dense SAE latents are persistent and often reflect intrinsically dense, functional residual-stream signals: position, context binding, entropy regulation, next-token letters, POS and PC1. These latents form antipodal pairs and shift from structural to output-oriented roles with depth. The authors add that context-binding latents challenge globally monosemantic directions. They caution that some dense latents may be noisy aggregates or a non-aligned basis, and that less than half are explained.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and intervenes on SAE latents in pretrained language models; it does not reproduce the original toy-network method. It uses residual-stream subspace ablation, latent geometry measurements, SAE-latent steering, and functional analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: Antipodality depends on SAE activation architecture: AbsoluteTopK eliminates antipodal dense latents. Dense-latent subspaces and feature classes vary by layer; latent density and ablation results are examined at different layer and dictionary settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Dense latents shift from structural (early) to semantic (mid) to output-oriented (late) roles. The dense subspaces form three layer clusters, and dense latents increase in the last two layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Intrinsically dense, non-sparse feature subspaces exist in LLM residual streams and change systematically with depth.

record.peer_reviewed: Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025; 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)
record.problems: The interpretability analysis primarily uses Gemma 2 2B JumpReLU SAEs with one dictionary size and sparsity constraint per layer. The authors say they have explained less than half of dense SAE features and do not establish that learned latents align with a true feature basis. Several figure-only results lack numerical values or uncertainty estimates; the context-binding judgments use an LLM judge. The authors also note possible noisy aggregation of sparse features and the difficulty of designing causal tests.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Detailed examples of individual position latents, additional POS-category plots, and supplementary visualizations of PC and subspace geometry were not given separate rows where the text did not report a distinct numerical or explicit outcome beyond the aggregate findings recorded above.

untested.parts: No toy models, no sparsity-dependent transition, no geometry of superposed features.
No test of neuron polysemanticity or of capacity competition.
No test of non-capacity sources of neuron polysemanticity.
Antipodal pairs show how SAEs encode signed directions. Nothing tests whether model features are 1-D or multi-dimensional.
Distribution of features across many neurons is not measured.
Completeness and cross-seed or cross-dictionary stability of sparse latents are not measured.

missing.what: Correct-flip rates for individual context-binding pairs: 81.5% (L13 15275/11449) and 76.5% (L12 14906/14599)
Dense-latent counts plateau by about 100k training steps and do not fall with longer training
Control: random non-dense latent subspaces have median principal angles near 90° across layers
PC1-aligned latent pair persists across L0 and dictionary sizes from 16k to 1m, with no added or removed PC-aligned latents
Multiple alphabet latents per letter at differing prefix specificity, attributed to feature splitting
Authors' argument that dense latents may span the true dense features without aligning with them, e.g. hard-to-separate period vs newline latents

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'supports V5' label for in-context rows is removed: local coherence is the baseline, not evidence of canonical units. V6 links are removed because antipodality concerns SAE encoding of signed directions, not feature dimensionality. Table 1 pairs were selected as highest-scoring by flips.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks or toy-model sparsity-dependent transition or regular geometry are tested.
The paper does not test whether neuron polysemanticity arises from competition for capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Context-binding SAE latents are not a test of whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.

The study examines SAE latents in real language models, not whether features are distributed across many neurons. Its principal analyses concern dense SAE latents rather than recovery of sparse-activating features.

The study examines selected dense SAE latents and explicitly notes that it does not establish whether SAE latents align with the true feature basis or provide a complete account of model representations.
The study measures antipodal pairs that reconstruct a one-dimensional line in SAE representations; it does not establish that all model features are one-dimensional.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Zero-ablated the subspace spanned by dense latents, then retrained an SAE.
rows.measure: High-density tail in retrained SAE latent activation-density distribution
rows.baseline: Original SAE and an SAE retrained after ablation of an equally sized non-dense-latent subspace
rows.value: Much fewer high-density latents than the original SAE and the non-dense ablation, in both dictionary sizes
rows.note: The authors interpret this as evidence that dense latents track a residual-stream subspace rather than being merely a training artifact.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured antipodality score for SAE latents and compared it with activation density.

conditions.value: majority of latents with activation frequency exceeding 0.3

rows.measure: Antipodality score; high scores indicate a paired latent with nearly opposite encoder and decoder directions
rows.baseline: not stated
rows.value: The majority of dense latents, particularly those with activation frequency exceeding 0.3, have pairwise scores greater than 0.9; density and score are strongly positively correlated
rows.note: The authors say the antipodal pair effectively allocates two latents to represent a one-dimensional line.
rows.check: Antipodal pairs mean two latents encode one signed direction, so latents are not one-to-one with model directions. That bears on V5, not V6: it does not test 1-D versus multi-dimensional model features. Dropped V4 and V6.

rows.note: No exact scores are stated for this configuration.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared TopK SAE with an AbsoluteTopK SAE that allows signed latent activations and selects by absolute activation.

conditions.value: same seed for the compared SAEs

rows.baseline: TopK SAE
rows.value: AbsoluteTopK eliminates antipodal dense latents
rows.note: The result shows antipodality depends on the activation architecture; AbsoluteTopK can use one latent direction in both positive and negative directions.
rows.check: AbsoluteTopK removes the antipodal pairs, so the latent set depends on the SAE activation function. This is architecture dependence of SAE units, not a reversal of V6. The layer is not stated in the text.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Computed Spearman correlations between latent decoder-direction projections and distances to text boundaries.
rows.measure: Correlation of dense-latent projections with sentence, paragraph, or context position
rows.baseline: not stated
rows.value: Sentence- and paragraph-tracking latents are prominent before layer 10; context-position tracking latents occur throughout the model
rows.note: Paragraph-tracking latents are reported as agnostic to artificially added formatting newlines, suggesting the newline measure acts as a proxy for semantic paragraph boundaries.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Steered generation along one member of an antipodal latent pair after ablating the pair's subspace; an LLM judge compared completions with feature-activating examples.

conditions.value: 2x the historical activation of that feature in that context

rows.measure: Fraction of flips from the unsteered judgment that align with the steering direction
rows.baseline: Unsteered generation and judgment
rows.value: The text reports reliable shifts toward the specific concept previously associated with the latent for several mid-layer pairs; Figure 5 gives the plotted results
rows.note: Intervention-induced result; it does not establish how often the model expresses these concepts without steering.
rows.check: Steering moves completions toward the in-context concept, so a latent's meaning is context-bound, not canonical. The value is not unreadable: Figs 18-19 give 81.5% and 76.5% correct flips for two pairs. Dropped V4.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured AUC-ROC for predicting dense-latent firing from grouped part-of-speech tags.

conditions.value: meaningful words: nouns, proper nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs

rows.measure: AUC-ROC of binary latent firing predicted by meaningful-word category
rows.baseline: not stated
rows.value: Approximately 0.8 for many dense latents in early layers
rows.note: The paper says narrower high-level POS categories alone did not achieve high AUC.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Selected latents whose top or bottom 100 logit contributions overwhelmingly correspond to tokens with a shared initial character.

conditions.value: at least 90% of the selected top or bottom 100 tokens start with the same character

rows.measure: Count and activation density of alphabet-related latents
rows.baseline: not stated
rows.value: 114 such latents; 21 have activation density >0.1, accounting for 20% of all dense latents; the paper says these occur as high-density features only at the final layer
rows.note: Examples in Table 2 include different specificity levels, from a single initial letter to longer prefixes.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured encoder-weight norm in the final 10 left singular directions of the unembedding matrix.

conditions.value: last 10 left singular vectors of WU

rows.measure: Fraction of latent encoder-weight norm in the subspace; proportion of aligned latents that are high-density
rows.baseline: not stated
rows.value: 99.6% of latents have α10 < 0.2; among those with α10 > 0.2, 75% are high-density and they account for 40% of high-density latents
rows.note: The authors call latents with α10 > 0.2 nullspace-aligned.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Ablated a latent decoder direction by setting its value to the decoder bias, then measured per-token output entropy.

conditions.value: 50 randomly selected latents, aggregated as a control group

rows.measure: Change in output entropy after direction ablation
rows.baseline: Randomly selected latent group
rows.value: Some nullspace latents cause much larger entropy shifts than the random baseline; latent 14325 has a disproportionate impact
rows.note: Exact entropy changes are not stated in the text.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Repeated the nullspace-latent ablation while freezing RMSNorm scaling.
rows.measure: Change in output entropy after direction ablation
rows.baseline: Ablation without frozen RMSNorm scaling
rows.value: The entropy change diminishes when RMSNorm scaling is frozen
rows.note: Supports a functional role for this direction in entropy modulation, with the effect depending on RMSNorm scaling.
rows.check: The diminished effect under frozen RMSNorm is the expected result of a mechanism check, not a partial effect.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured dense-latent cosine similarity with the first principal component and norm share in the top five principal components.
rows.measure: Alignment of dense latents with principal components
rows.baseline: not stated
rows.value: An antipodal pair consistently reconstructs most of the first PC, with cosine similarity > 0.75; most other dense latents place little norm in the top five PCs
rows.note: The authors say the pair is not immediately interpretable and that the PC-alignment pattern persists across tested SAE sparsity targets and dictionary sizes.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured layerwise fractions of SAE latents above several activation-density thresholds.
rows.measure: Fraction of latents above each density threshold
rows.baseline: Middle layers 5–23
rows.value: Early layers 0–4 show transient spikes just above 0.05 and 0.1; fractions are remarkably stable across layers 5–23; the last two layers show an increase in dense latents
rows.note: The authors attribute early fluctuations mainly to training variability and identify an increase before unembedding.
rows.check: Layerwise density counts do not test whether SAEs recover model features.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared explanations generated from activating and non-activating phrases sampled from the same context or across a corpus.
rows.measure: Specificity and consistency of generated latent explanations
rows.baseline: Sparse-latent explanations sampled in-context and across contexts
rows.value: Dense-latent explanations are specific but highly diverse across contexts; all-context explanations become vague or generic. Sparse-latent explanations center around a similar theme across both sampling methods
rows.note: The authors acknowledge that explanations may overfit context and that an abstract, uninterpretable feature remains a possible interpretation.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared pairwise principal angles between subspaces spanned by dense latents at different layers.
rows.measure: Median principal angles between dense-latent subspaces
rows.baseline: not stated
rows.value: Three clusters: layers 0–4 share a dense subspace, layers 10–22 share another, and the final layers change markedly relative to earlier layers
rows.note: Layer-dependent subspaces qualify any claim that these representations form a single stable basis throughout the model.
rows.check: Dense subspaces differing across layers reflect residual-stream change across depth, not SAE-unit instability.

relationships.condition: Dense-subspace ablation and retraining (Gemma 2 2B L25, GPT-2 Small, LLaMA-3.2-1B final layer); dense-latent taxonomy in Gemma 2 2B
relationships.reason: Ablating the dense subspace removes dense latents on retraining, while a sparse-subspace ablation does not (R01-R04). Latents track position, POS, next-token letters and entropy (R10, R34-R38).
relationships.display_finding: Ablating the dense subspace removed dense latents on retraining, while ablating a sparse subspace did not. The dense latents tracked position, part of speech, next-token letters and entropy.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R01, R03, and R04 establish intrinsically dense structure, but do not test whether recoverable sparse features also exist. V4 does not assert that all representations are sparse; unexplained dense latents likewise do not establish a limitation of that stated claim.

relationships.condition: Context-binding dense latent pairs, Gemma Scope layers 12-17
relationships.reason: Unclear-judgment rates rise from 0.02-0.05 in context to 0.53-0.80 out of context (R12-R33). Dense-latent explanations diverge across contexts, unlike sparse latents (R41). Steering effects are context-bound (R11).

relation.reason: Its own ablations, geometry measurements, interpretation comparisons, and interventions examine recovered representations and SAE-unit stability.

tranche.reason: The study presents results and arguments requiring qualification of assumptions about sparse, globally meaningful SAE units.

source_check.notes: The checked text is arXiv v2, dated 5 November 2025. Context-binding remains an interpretation rather than a proven binding mechanism; the authors explain less than half of dense latents and caution that learned bases may mix underlying features.

statements.correction: Gemma 2 2B layer 25 and GPT-2 Small/LLaMA-3.2-1B final-layer dense-subspace ablations suppress dense latents after retraining; non-dense controls retain the high-density tail. This establishes additional dense structure, without showing that recoverable sparse features are absent.
statements.problem: The ablation findings are accurate, but dense recovered structure does not contradict V4's stated existence claim about recoverable sparse features.

statements.correction: TopK and JumpReLU dense latents form antipodal pairs; AbsoluteTopK permits signed activations and eliminates the pairing. V5 limits_scope for this activation-function comparison.
statements.problem: The architecture comparison is accurate; its appropriate condition-specific label is limits_scope because the recovered pairing depends on the activation function.

reader_labels.reason: Dense latents have high antipodality scores, often exceeding 0.9 for latents with activation frequency above 0.3, and the authors interpret pairs as representing a one-dimensional line (R05–R08).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The antipodal pairs disappear when signed latent activations are allowed, so the observed paired geometry depends on SAE activation architecture (R09).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Context-binding dense latents and layerwise dense-subspace comparisons in Gemma 2 2B
reader_labels.reason: In-context explanations and judgments are coherent, but explanations vary across contexts and out-of-context examples yield much higher unclear rates; dense subspaces also change across layer groups. This limits claims that SAE latents are complete, stable, canonical units (R12–R33, R41–R42).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Same-context examples for the tested context-binding pairs
reader_labels.reason: For all 11 listed pairs, the fraction of unclear judgments is low for in-context examples, consistent with locally coherent features even though this does not demonstrate globally canonical units (R12, R14, R16, R18, R20, R22, R24, R26, R28, R30, R32).
